1.text:
What Powers the Sun?

Welcome to Quarter 3, where the story moves from our own planet out to the stars. And we start with the one star we can actually study up close: our Sun. It formed about 4.6 billion years ago, and every day it lights and warms the whole Earth from about 150 million km away.

This deck chases one big question: what powers the Sun, and how does its energy reach Earth? Along the way we'll go inside the Sun, watch hydrogen turn into helium, meet storms that can knock out satellites, and see how the Sun changes over its long life.

Did you know? The sunlight hitting your desk right now left the Sun's surface about 8.3 minutes ago.

2.text:
Today I Can...

This is your checklist for this deck. Copy these into your notebook as "I can" statements and rate yourself at the end.

I can describe the Sun's size, mass, power and temperatures. I can model the Sun's six layers, from core to corona. I can explain how gravity and gas pressure stay balanced. I can explain how fusion turns 4 hydrogen into 1 helium plus energy, using E = mc². I can trace energy out by radiation and convection all the way to Earth.

I can also use neutrinos and helioseismology as evidence for what's inside, explain sunspots and the 11-year cycle as magnetism, explain how CMEs and our magnetosphere shape space weather, explain how sunlight drives Earth's systems, and describe how the Sun brightens and ages, ending as a red giant and not a supernova. Some of these match Indiana standards ES.2.3, ES.6.2 and ES.1.4, and a few are extra enrichment.

3.text:
The Sun by the Numbers

Time for some big numbers. The Sun's luminosity, the total power it gives off every second, is 3.828 × 1026 watts. Its radius is 695,700 km, about 109 Earths lined up side by side. See the tiny dot on the slide? That's Earth drawn to scale.

The Sun's mass is 332,900 Earths, which is 99.8% of all the mass in the solar system. Everything else, every planet, moon, asteroid and comet, is the leftover 0.2%. Its surface sits at 5,772 K, and its core is about 15 million K.

Even with all that mass, the Sun's average density is only about a quarter of Earth's. That's because it's made of gas, in a hot charged form called plasma, not rock.

Did you know? About 1.3 million Earths could fit inside the Sun.

4.text:
Six Layers, Inside Out

Like an onion, the Sun has layers. Start in the middle: the core, about 15 million K, where fusion happens. Around it is the radiative zone, where energy moves outward as light. Next is the convective zone, where hot gas rises and cool gas sinks, like soup simmering on a stove.

Then comes the photosphere. This is the visible surface, the layer where sunlight finally escapes into space, at 5,772 K. Above it lies the thin, reddish chromosphere at about 10,000 K. And on the outside is the corona, the Sun's wispy outer atmosphere, at 1 to 2 million K.

Notice something weird? The temperature drops from the core to the surface, then shoots back up in the chromosphere and corona. The outer atmosphere is hundreds of times hotter than the surface below it.

Did you know? The bubbly pattern on the photosphere, called granulation, is the tops of convection cells. Each granule lasts only about 5 to 10 minutes.

5.text:
Gravity In, Pressure Out

The Sun is a huge ball of gas, so why doesn't gravity crush it into a tiny lump? The answer is hydrostatic equilibrium: gravity pulling in balances gas pressure pushing out.

Think of a balloon. The air inside pushes out, the rubber pulls in, and the balloon settles at the size where the two balance. The Sun does the same thing at every depth. The deeper you go, the more weight of gas sits above you, so the pressure has to be greater. At the center, the pressure reaches 2.477 × 1011 bar, hundreds of billions of times the air pressure on Earth.

This balance also works like a thermostat. If fusion ran too fast, the extra heat would make the core expand and cool, slowing fusion down. If it ran too slow, the core would shrink and heat up, speeding fusion up. That keeps the Sun steady for billions of years.

Did you know? Before fusion was understood, Kelvin and Helmholtz guessed the Sun shines by slowly shrinking. That could only power it for tens of millions of years, much shorter than Earth's age of 4.54 billion years.

6.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 1

Quick check before we head into the core. What keeps the Sun from collapsing?

Is it A) its solid iron core, B) gas pressure balancing gravity, C) the solar wind blowing outward, or D) its fast spin? Look back at Slides 3 to 5, pick one, and be ready to explain why the other three don't work.

7.text:
The Proton-Proton Chain

Nuclear fusion means light nuclei joining into a heavier nucleus. In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei (single protons) fuse into helium through a three-step recipe called the proton-proton chain.

Step 1: two hydrogen nuclei fuse into deuterium (²H, one proton plus one neutron). One proton turns into a neutron and spits out a positron and a neutrino. Step 2: deuterium grabs another proton and becomes helium-3 (³He), giving off a gamma ray. Steps 1 and 2 each happen twice. Step 3: two helium-3 nuclei smash together to make helium-4 (⁴He) and release two protons back into the core.

The net result: four hydrogen nuclei make one helium-4 nucleus, plus energy. Why only in the core? Protons are all positive, so they push each other away. Only at around 15 million K are they moving fast enough to get close and stick.

Did you know? A positron is an antimatter electron. As soon as it meets an ordinary electron, the two destroy each other and become pure gamma-ray energy.

8.text:
Mass Becomes Sunlight

The trick behind fusion is that the helium you make weighs less than the hydrogen you started with. Four hydrogen atoms have a mass of 4.03130 u (atomic mass units). One helium atom has a mass of only 4.00260 u.

That leaves 0.02870 u missing, about 0.7% of the starting mass. It didn't vanish. It turned into energy, following Einstein's famous E = mc². Since c, the speed of light, is a huge number, and it gets squared, even a tiny bit of mass becomes an enormous amount of energy.

That's why fusion can keep the Sun shining for billions of years, while shrinking or burning could not.

Did you know? Fusing just 1 kg of hydrogen releases about 6.4 × 1014 joules, roughly what a large power plant makes in a week.

9.text:
The Sun Loses Mass Every Second

Every second, the Sun turns 4.26 million tonnes of mass into energy. To do that, it fuses about 600 million tonnes of hydrogen into helium each second, and the missing 0.7% becomes light. That light streams out at 3.828 × 1026 W, the same luminosity you saw on Slide 3.

You can check the math yourself. Multiply the mass lost per second, 4.26 × 109 kg, by c², (3.00 × 108 m/s)², and you get about 3.83 × 1026 W. The numbers match!

Will the Sun shrink away to nothing? Not even close. Over its whole life so far, it has lost only about 0.03% of its mass this way.

Did you know? The solar wind carries away another 1 to 2 million tons of matter every second, on top of the mass lost to fusion.

10.text:
Light Takes the Slow Road Out

Energy made in the core has a long trip ahead. In the radiative zone, a photon of light travels only a tiny distance before an atom absorbs it and sends a new photon off in a random direction. This zigzag path is called a random walk, and it takes about 170,000 years. Estimates range from 10,000 to 1 million years because scientists use different models.

Starting at about 71% of the way out, the gas changes jobs. Convection takes over: hot gas rises, cools at the top, and sinks back down, like a pot of boiling pasta water.

Finally the energy leaves the photosphere as sunlight. From there it needs only about 8.3 minutes to reach Earth. Thousands of years to escape the Sun, eight minutes to cross 150 million km!

Did you know? Imagine trying to leave a packed stadium where every person you bump into spins you in a random direction. That's roughly a photon's life in the radiative zone.

11.text:
Neutrinos: A Direct Look at the Core

Light takes thousands of years to escape, so how can we see the core as it is right now? With neutrinos. A neutrino is a nearly massless particle made in the proton-proton chain that flies straight out of the core. They pass straight through Earth, and through you.

About 6.5 × 1014 solar neutrinos zip through every square meter each second. That's 65 billion through every square centimeter, about the size of your fingernail. Because they barely interact with anything, detectors must be huge and buried deep underground to shield them from other particles.

In the 1970s, Raymond Davis's experiment found only 1/3 of the expected neutrinos. That puzzle lasted for decades. In 2002, the SNO detector counted all 3 types of neutrino, and the total matched predictions. Neutrinos change type on their way here.

Did you know? A neutrino leaves the Sun's core and reaches Earth in about 8 minutes, giving us a live report from the center of the Sun.

12.text:
The Sun Rings Like a Bell

The Sun never sits still. Its surface bobs up and down about every 5 minutes, driven by sound waves trapped inside. Helioseismology is the study of these vibrations to map the Sun's inside, just like geologists use earthquake waves to map Earth's interior.

Each wave follows a different path. Shallow sound paths sample the outer layers, and deep paths dive toward the core. By combining millions of waves, scientists measured that the base of the convection zone sits at 0.713 of the Sun's radius.

The GONG network uses 6 sites around the world, so someone always has the Sun in view, 24 hours a day. Sound waves cross from the center to the surface in about 1 hour, so this method, like neutrinos, tells us about the Sun as it is now.

Did you know? You can't hear the Sun ring. Sound can't travel through empty space, so the "music" is detected as tiny back-and-forth Doppler shifts in sunlight.

13.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 2

Time to test the big idea. Where does the Sun's energy come from?

Is it A) burning hydrogen gas with oxygen, B) mass lost when 4 H fuse into 1 He, C) the Sun slowly shrinking, or D) radioactive uranium in the core? Think back to Slides 5, 7 and 8. Choose one and explain why each of the others fails.

14.text:
Sunspots Are Magnetic

A sunspot is a cooler, darker patch where strong magnetism blocks convection. Remember, convection carries heat up to the surface. Where magnetic fields poke through, they hold back the rising hot gas, so that patch cools off.

Sunspots have a dark center called the umbra, at about 3,800 K, which is still very hot and bright, and a lighter fringe called the penumbra. The surrounding photosphere is 5,772 K, so the spot only looks dark by comparison. Magnetic fields in a sunspot are about 3,000 gauss, thousands of times stronger than Earth's field.

Spots often come in pairs, one north (N) and one south (S). They are the two ends of a magnetic loop that has burst through the surface, like a garden hose arching out of the ground.

Did you know? If you could cut out a sunspot and put it alone in the night sky, it would shine about as bright as the full Moon.

15.text:
The 11-Year Sunspot Cycle

The number of sunspots rises and falls in a cycle. On average, it takes 11 years to go from one peak to the next. The graph shows the yearly sunspot number climbing and falling between 2008, 2014, 2019 and 2024.

Cycle 24 peaked in April 2014. Cycle 25 reached its maximum in October 2024, and now the numbers are falling. Scientists number these cycles, starting with Cycle 1 in 1755.

There's a twist. Each cycle, the Sun's magnetic poles flip. North becomes south and south becomes north. So the full magnetic pattern takes 22 years to repeat, two sunspot cycles.

Did you know? Even at the busiest peak of a cycle, sunspots cover less than half of one percent of the Sun's surface.

16.text:
Graph the Solar Cycle

Your turn to be the scientist. Here's real data from NOAA SWPC and WDC-SILSO, the yearly averages of monthly sunspot numbers.

2014: 113.6. 2015: 69.8. 2016: 39.8. 2017: 21.8. 2018: 7.0. 2019: 3.6. 2020: 8.8. 2021: 29.5. 2022: 83.0. 2023: 125.3. 2024: 154.5. 2025: 123.4.

On graph paper, plot year against sunspot number. For each year, mark whether the count went up or down. Circle the minimum and the two peaks. How many years are there from peak to peak, and how does that compare with 11? Then make a prediction: when will Cycle 26 begin?

17.text:
Flares and CMEs

The tangled magnetic fields around sunspots can snap and release huge amounts of energy. Two kinds of blasts come out. A solar flare is a sudden burst of light. Because it travels at the speed of light, flare light reaches Earth in about 8 minutes.

A coronal mass ejection, or CME, is a huge cloud of plasma and magnetic field thrown out of the corona. It can carry billions of tons of material. CMEs are much slower than light, taking from 15 hours to several days to reach Earth.

Meanwhile, the Sun is always blowing a steady stream of particles called the solar wind, at about 400 km/s. Earth and its magnetosphere sit right in the path of all of it.

Did you know? Flares are classed A, B, C, M and X, and each letter is ten times stronger than the one before.

18.text:
Space Weather Reaches Earth

On May 10, 2024, a string of CMEs slammed into Earth. The result was a G5 geomagnetic storm, the top of NOAA's scale and the first G5 storm since October 2003.

When CMEs arrive, the effects pile up. Auroras were seen far south of where they normally show up. GPS and radio signals got errors. Satellites felt extra drag as the upper atmosphere heated and puffed up. Power grids felt strain from currents induced in long power lines.

Our main protection is Earth's magnetic field. The magnetopause, the outer edge of our magnetosphere, shields us by turning most of the charged particles aside. This links straight back to Deck 11, where you learned about the magnetosphere and auroras.

Did you know? During the May 2024 storm, people in places like Florida and southern Texas snapped photos of the northern lights.

19.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 3

A fast CME leaves the Sun right now. When could it reach Earth?

Is it A) in about 8 minutes, B) in about 15 to 18 hours, C) in about 2 months, or D) never, because the magnetosphere stops it far away? Look back at Slides 17 and 18 and pick your answer. Be ready to say what kind of solar blast matches each of the other choices.

20.text:
Sunlight Runs Earth's Systems

At the top of Earth's atmosphere, sunlight delivers 1,361 W/m². That's like having more than thirteen 100-watt light bulbs shining on every square meter.

Not all of it stays. About 29% is reflected back to space, mostly by clouds, snow and ice. Scientists call this reflectiveness albedo, and Earth's is 0.294. The rest is absorbed and goes to work.

That absorbed sunlight drives evaporation and the water cycle. It powers winds and ocean currents, because the equator gets heated more than the poles. It feeds photosynthesis, the start of nearly every food chain. And it warms land, sea and air. Almost everything that moves on Earth's surface is solar powered.

Did you know? Averaged over the whole globe, day and night, Earth gets only about one-fourth of that number, about 340 W/m².

21.text:
The Sun Brightens with Age

The Sun hasn't always shone like it does today. When Earth was young, the Sun was only about 70% as bright as today. As hydrogen in the core turns to helium, the core slowly squeezes and heats up, so fusion speeds up and the Sun gets brighter.

Follow the timeline. The Sun forms at 0 Gyr (billion years). Earth forms 4.54 Gyr ago. Today we sit a little less than halfway through the Sun's main sequence, which lasts about 10 Gyr. In about 1 Gyr from now, the Sun will be bright enough to boil Earth's oceans.

Near the end, the Sun will swell into a red giant, then shrink into a white dwarf. It won't explode as a supernova. Medium stars like the Sun don't have enough mass for that.

Did you know? A dimmer young Sun creates a puzzle called the faint young Sun paradox: early Earth should have frozen, but rocks show liquid water nearly 4 billion years ago.

22.text:
Model the Sun: Layers and Life Span

Now build it yourself. This task matches Indiana standard ES.2.3, and it has two parts on one page.

Part A is a cutaway model. Draw all 6 layers, each with its temperature. In the core, show 4 H fusing into 1 He plus energy. Draw a zigzag through the radiative zone and convection loops near the top. Show light leaving toward Earth in 8.3 minutes.

Part B is a life span strip. Start with the Sun's birth 4.6 Gyr ago as a dimmer Sun. Mark today, with Earth beside it. Show the Sun brightening over time, then becoming a red giant, then a white dwarf. Mark "no supernova" and explain why. When you're done, explain the energy path out loud to a partner.

23.text:
Check for Understanding: Part 4

This one bothered scientists for a long time. Why was the faint young Sun a puzzle?

Is it A) the young Sun was too hot for life, B) early Earth had liquid water anyway, C) the young Sun had no core yet, or D) Earth was much closer to the Sun? Look back at Slides 20 and 21 and choose. Then think about which numbers would need to change to keep early Earth warm.

24.text:
Exit Ticket

You've traveled from the core to the corona and back to Earth. Show what you know with three questions.

First, trace sunlight from the core to your skin, and name 3 layers it crosses. Second, why does the Sun lose about 4 million tonnes of mass each second? Third, how does Earth's magnetosphere protect satellites from a CME?

When you're done, look back at your "I can" list from Slide 2 and rate yourself 1 to 3 on each one.

25.text:
The Standards Behind This Lesson

This lesson follows the Indiana Earth and Space Science standards. Here's what they ask, in plain words.

ES.2.3: build a model of the Sun's layers and life span. Explain how fusion in the core makes elements and energy, how that energy is carried by convection and sent out into space, including to Earth, by radiation. It also says elements heavier than iron only form in supernovae, but scientists now know more. Elements up to iron are made by fusion in stars, and supernovae make a lot of iron and spread these elements. About half of the elements heavier than iron are made by slow neutron capture (the s-process) in aging giant stars, and most of the rest by fast neutron capture (the r-process) in neutron star mergers and possibly rare supernovae. You'll see that part in Deck 17.

ES.6.2: explain how Earth's fluid outer core creates the magnetosphere and how it helps protect people and technology like satellites from the solar wind. ES.1.4 is introduced here: compare the life cycles of low, medium (like our Sun) and high mass stars on the Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram, including which ones become red giants and which go supernova. You'll dig into that in Decks 15 and 17.
